claim: HID-1 is a highly conserved protein with homologs in Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila melanogaster, mouse, and Homo sapiens, but not in budding yeast.
source: The Hid1 gene encodes a highly conserved protein (HID-1) that has homologs in Drosophila melanogaster, mouse, and Homo sapiens, but not in budding yeast.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction section of the manuscript.

claim: Conditional knockout of HID-1 in pancreatic β cells leads to glucose intolerance in mice.
source: A conditional knockout of HID-1 in pancreatic β cells leads to glucose intolerance and a remarkable increase in the serum proinsulin/insulin ratio caused by defective proinsulin processing.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Hid1-betaKO mice exhibited higher basal glucose levels than RIP-Cre mice during glucose-tolerance testing at 10-12 weeks of age.
source: At 10–12 weeks of age, Hid1-betaKOmice exhibited higher basal glucose levels and glucose intolerance than RIP-Cre mice during glucose-tolerance testing (GTT, Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1F showing blood glucose measurements during GTT.

claim: Hid1-betaKO mice performed normally in insulin-tolerance testing.
source: However, Hid1-betaKO mice performed normally in insulin-tolerance testing (ITT) (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: HID-1 protein was greatly reduced in islets isolated from Hid1-betaKO mice compared to age-matched RIP-Cre mice.
source: As demonstrated in Figure 1B, HID-1 protein was greatly reduced in islets isolated from Hid1-betaKOmice compared to that in age-matched RIP-Cre mice, which were used thereafter as wild-type (WT) controls.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Western blot data in Figure 1B.

claim: The remaining expression of HID-1 in KO islets was only 20% of that from WT islets.
source: The remaining expression of HID-1 in KO islets was only 20% of that from WT islets (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: HID-1 was highly expressed in pancreatic β cells, but only weakly expressed in α cells.
source: By positive immunofluorescence staining, we verified that HID-1 was highly expressed in pancreatic β cells, but only weakly expressed in α cells (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hid1-betaKO mice showed no obvious phenotype with respect to body weight.
source: Hid1-betaKOmice are viable and fertile, and the mice showed no obvious phenotype with respect to body weight (Figure 1E), feeding, mating performance and overall behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by body weight comparison data in Figure 1E.

claim: Impaired glucose tolerance in Hid1-betaKO mice may be caused by insufficient insulin release.
source: These results indicate that impaired glucose tolerance may be caused by insufficient insulin release.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the text based on the glucose tolerance and insulin tolerance test results.

claim: The islet size in KO mice was not significantly different from that in WT mice.
source: Quantification indicated that the islet size (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) and the density of the islets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) in KOmice were not significantly different from those of in WT mice.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by quantification data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The density of β cells was similar in WT and KO mice.
source: Furthermore, the general morphology of β cells identified with proinsulin staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) and the density of β cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E) were similar in the WT and KO mice.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: No significant difference was observed between WT and KO β cells for either Ca2+ influx or the Ca2+-induced Cm increase.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3, no significant difference was observed between WT and KO β cells for either Ca2+ influx or the Ca2+-induced Cm increase.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by membrane capacitance measurement data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: HID-1 is not required for the exocytosis of SGs per se in either mouse or worm.
source: Consistent with the fact that HID-1 is not required for SG exocytosis, hid-1 mutants did not block secretion of a DCV cargo (AEX-5-VENUS) in C. elegans (Mesa et al., 2011). Collectively, these results suggest that HID-1 is not required for the exocytosis of SGs per se in either mouse or worm.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by both the current study's data and a citation to previous work in C. elegans.

claim: The serum proinsulin level was markedly elevated from 5 pM in WT mice to 78 pM in Hid1-betaKO mice.
source: Interestingly, the serum proinsulin level was markedly elevated from 5 pM in WT mice to 78 pM in Hid1-betaKOmice (Figure 2A), whereas the basal insulin level was only slightly increased (150 ± 29 pM for WT and 198 ± 39 pM for KO mice).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The ratio between proinsulin and insulin increased from 3.3% in WT mice to 39.4% in KO mice.
source: The ratio between proinsulin and insulin was determined to be 3.3%, consistent with previous reports (Wijesekara et al., 2010; Zhu et al., 2002). This value increased to 39.4% in KO mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2B, with citations to previous reports for the WT value.

claim: Isolated size-matched islets from Hid1-betaKO mice released much less insulin in response to glucose stimulation.
source: We found that isolated size-matched islets from Hid1-betaKO mice released much less insulin (Figure 2C), but more proinsulin (Figure 2D), in response to glucose stimulation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by glucose-stimulated insulin secretion data in Figure 2C.

claim: Isolated size-matched islets from Hid1-betaKO mice released more proinsulin in response to glucose stimulation.
source: We found that isolated size-matched islets from Hid1-betaKO mice released much less insulin (Figure 2C), but more proinsulin (Figure 2D), in response to glucose stimulation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by glucose-stimulated proinsulin secretion data in Figure 2D.

claim: Pan-neuronal ablation of HID-1 failed to increase proinsulin in the serum.
source: Pan-neuronal ablation of HID-1 failed to increase proinsulin in the serum (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the elevated proinsulin phenotype was mainly due to lack of HID-1 function in pancreatic β cells.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The elevated proinsulin phenotype was mainly due to lack of HID-1 function in pancreatic β cells.
source: Pan-neuronal ablation of HID-1 failed to increase proinsulin in the serum (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the elevated proinsulin phenotype was mainly due to lack of HID-1 function in pancreatic β cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the text based on the comparison between RIP-Cre and Nestin-Cre knockout experiments.

claim: Islets from Hid1-betaKO mice contained a lower level of mature insulin but an elevated level of proinsulin compared with WT islets.
source: Western blot analysis demonstrated that islets from Hid1-betaKO mice contained a lower level of mature insulin but an elevated level of proinsulin compared with WT islets (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Western blot data in Figure 3A.

claim: A higher amount of proinsulin and delayed processing of proinsulin was observed in Hid1-betaKO mice during pulse-chase experiments.
source: We observed a higher amount of proinsulin and delayed processing of proinsulin in Hid1-betaKO mice (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by pulse-chase experiment data in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: The insulin/proinsulin ratio was significantly lower in KO islets than in WT controls during the chase period.
source: As a consequence, the insulin/proinsulin ratio was significantly lower in KO islets than in WT controls during the chase period (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3D.

claim: HID-1 KO rat INS-1 cells showed slower processing of Proinsulin1 and delayed production of mature Insulin1.
source: As shown in Figure 3F and 3G, LC-MS detected slower processing of Proinsulin1 and delayed production of mature Insulin1 in the KO INS-1 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by LC-MS data in Figure 3F and 3G.

claim: The insulin/proinsulin ratio was significantly lower in the KO INS-1 cells than in WT controls during the chase period.
source: The insulin/proinsulin ratio was significantly lower in the KO cells than in WT controls during the chase period (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3H.

claim: HID-1 KO caused a slight decrease in PC1/3 and PC2 levels, but not in CPE levels.
source: Quantification showed that HID-1 KO caused a slight decrease in PC1/3 and PC2 levels, but not in CPE levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Western blot quantification data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The slight decrease in PC1/3 and PC2 levels is not sufficient to explain the drastic defect in proinsulin processing.
source: A previous study demonstrated that the 50% reduction in PC1/3 only elevated serum proinsulin/insulin ratio to 0.12 (Zhu et al., 2002), hence, the slight decrease in PC1/3 and PC2 levels that we observed is not sufficient to explain the drastic defect in proinsulin processing (proinsulin/insulin ratio of 0.39).
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the text, comparing the current findings with a cited previous study.

claim: A dispersed distribution of proinsulin throughout the HID-1 KO cells was observed, unlike the perinuclear localization seen in WT cells.
source: Interestingly, we observed a dispersed distribution of proinsulin throughout the HID-1 KO cells, which was unlike the perinuclear localization seen in WT cells (Figure 4A, see also Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence imaging data in Figure 4A.

claim: The density of proinsulin vesicles was significantly increased from 0.58 ± 0.10/µm3 in WT cells to 0.99 ± 0.07/µm3 in KO cells.
source: The density of proinsulin vesicles was significantly increased from 0.58 ± 0.10/µm3 in WT cells to 0.99 ± 0.07/µm3 in KO cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by quantification data in Figure 4B.

claim: Proinsulin is a specific ISG marker.
source: Since proinsulin is a specific ISG marker, the increase in proinsulin signals may reflect an increase in the number of ISGs.
evidence: This is stated in the text as established knowledge.

claim: VAMP4 recruitment to or retention in ISG depends on HID-1.
source: Thus, proinsulin-positive ISGs in HID-1 KO cells seem to retain Syt-IV but not VAMP4, suggesting that VAMP4 recruitment to r retention in ISG depends on HID-1.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the text based on the co-localization data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were many more granules with a lighter dense core in KO cells than in WT cells for both peripheral and Golgi regions.
source: Adopting the same separation of grey level as for WT cells, we found that there were many more granules with a lighter dense core (<190) in KO cells than in WT cells for both peripheral (47.6% vs 0.8%) and Golgi (87.8% vs 11.7%) regions, suggesting the appearance of more ISGs in both regions in the absence of HID-1.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of FIB-SEM data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: HID-1 deficiency significantly decreased the size of SGs in the peripheral region.
source: However, HID-1 deficiency significantly decreased the size of SGs in the peripheral region (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2F,G), suggesting abnormal maturation of SGs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by size distribution data in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2F,G.

claim: A low frequency of homotypic fusion events (8.2 ± 0.8 per 1000 SGs) was observed in WT β cells, mostly near the Golgi region.
source: We observed a low frequency of homotypic fusion events (8.2 ± 0.8 per 1000 SGs) in WT β cells, mostly near the Golgi region, which was significantly reduced by ~ 8 fold (1.2 ± 0.4 per 1000 SGs) in HID-1 KO cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by FIB-SEM data quantified in Figure 5B.

claim: The frequency of homotypic fusion events was significantly reduced by ~ 8 fold in HID-1 KO cells compared to WT cells.
source: We observed a low frequency of homotypic fusion events (8.2 ± 0.8 per 1000 SGs) in WT β cells, mostly near the Golgi region, which was significantly reduced by ~ 8 fold (1.2 ± 0.4 per 1000 SGs) in HID-1 KO cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by FIB-SEM data quantified in Figure 5B.

claim: About 7.7% of ISGs derived from WT cells underwent fusion in the in vitro fusion assay.
source: About 7.7% of ISGs derived from WT cells underwent fusion, while the fraction decreased to 0.89% for ISGs derived from HID-1 KO cells, which was as low as that for negative controls in which ATP was depleted or the reaction system was placed on ice (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by in vitro fusion assay data in Figure 5F.

claim: The fraction of ISGs that underwent fusion decreased to 0.89% for ISGs derived from HID-1 KO cells.
source: About 7.7% of ISGs derived from WT cells underwent fusion, while the fraction decreased to 0.89% for ISGs derived from HID-1 KO cells, which was as low as that for negative controls in which ATP was depleted or the reaction system was placed on ice (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by in vitro fusion assay data in Figure 5F.

claim: HID-1 deficiency blocks homotypic fusion of ISGs.
source: Taken together, both EM and fluorescence co-localization assays support the conclusion that HID-1 deficiency blocks homotypic fusion of ISGs.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on multiple lines of evidence from FIB-SEM and in vitro fusion assays.

claim: The granular DAMP intensities displayed a significant shift to smaller values in HID-1 KO β cells compared with WT cells.
source: The granular DAMP intensities displayed a significant shift to smaller values in HID-1 KO β cells compared with WT cells (Figure 6B), suggesting that HID-1 deficiency blocks acidification at the single granule level.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by DAMP intensity distribution data in Figure 6B.

claim: HID-1 deficiency blocks acidification at the single granule level.
source: The granular DAMP intensities displayed a significant shift to smaller values in HID-1 KO β cells compared with WT cells (Figure 6B), suggesting that HID-1 deficiency blocks acidification at the single granule level.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the text based on DAMP intensity measurements.

claim: DAMP levels in HID-1 KO β cells were significantly reduced to an average of 57.3% of those in WT β-cells.
source: DAMP levels in HID-1 KO β cells were significantly reduced to an average of 57.3% of those in WT β-cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6C.

claim: SG acidification is disturbed in the absence of HID-1.
source: These data suggest that SG acidification is disturbed in the absence of HID-1.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on DAMP and Lysosensor measurements.

claim: Homotypic fusion of ISGs has been observed in several neuroendocrine cells, including PC12 cells, pituitary cells and mast cells.
source: Homotypic fusion of ISGs has been observed in several neuroendocrine cells, including PC12 cells (Ahras et al., 2006; Tooze et al., 2001; Wendler et al., 2001), pituitary cells (Farquhar and Palade, 1981) and mast cells (Hammel and Meilijson, 2015), and in the formation of large dense core vesicles in yeast (Asensio et al., 2013), but it has not been observed in pancreatic β cells (Arvan and Halban, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to previous studies.

claim: Homotypic fusion of ISGs has not been observed in pancreatic β cells according to previous reports.
source: Homotypic fusion of ISGs has been observed in several neuroendocrine cells, including PC12 cells (Ahras et al., 2006; Tooze et al., 2001; Wendler et al., 2001), pituitary cells (Farquhar and Palade, 1981) and mast cells (Hammel and Meilijson, 2015), and in the formation of large dense core vesicles in yeast (Asensio et al., 2013), but it has not been observed in pancreatic β cells (Arvan and Halban, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to a previous study.

claim: ISG homotypic fusion is dependent on NSF and α-SNAP.
source: An in vitro fusion assay has revealed that ISG homotypic fusion is dependent on NSF and α-SNAP (Urbe et al., 1998) and on the SNARE protein syntaxin 6 (STX6), but not on syntaxin 1 or SNAP-25 (Wendler et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to previous studies.

claim: ISG homotypic fusion is dependent on the SNARE protein syntaxin 6 (STX6), but not on syntaxin 1 or SNAP-25.
source: An in vitro fusion assay has revealed that ISG homotypic fusion is dependent on NSF and α-SNAP (Urbe et al., 1998) and on the SNARE protein syntaxin 6 (STX6), but not on syntaxin 1 or SNAP-25 (Wendler et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Syt-IV localizes to ISGs and is involved in SG maturation.
source: It has been suggested that Syt-IV, a synaptotagmin protein that interacts with SNAREs, localizes to ISGs and is involved in SG maturation (Ahras et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to a previous study.

claim: The gene hid-1 was identified during a search for mutants with a high-temperature-induced dauer formation (Hid) phenotype in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: A gene designated as hid-1 was identified during a search for mutants with a high-temperature-induced dauer formation (Hid) phenotype in Caenorhabditis elegans (Ailion and Thomas, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to the original study.

claim: hid-1 has been isolated by a genetic screen for mutants mislocalizing rabphilin (RBF-1 in C. elegans).
source: Subsequently, hid-1 has been isolated by a genetic screen for mutants mislocalizing rabphilin (RBF-1 in C. elegans), an effector of RAB-27 that is involved in SG exocytosis (Mesa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to a previous study.

claim: HID-1 shares no homology domains with other proteins but is suggested to be a membrane-attached protein that shuttles between membrane and cytosol.
source: HID-1 shares no homology domains with other proteins but is suggested to be a membrane-attached protein that shuttles between membrane and cytosol (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Recent studies in C. elegans have suggested an essential role for HID-1 in neuropeptide signaling.
source: Recent studies in C. elegans have suggested an essential role for HID-1 in neuropeptide signaling (Mesa et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2011), but the exact site(s) of action and the molecular mechanism by which HID-1 acts remain unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to previous studies.

claim: Loss of function of HID-1 in mice leads to diabetes-like symptoms characterized by glucose intolerance, insufficient insulin release, and elevated proinsulin secretion.
source: We demonstrate that HID-1 is a novel factor required for homotypic fusion of ISGs. Loss of function of HID-1 in mice leads to diabetes-like symptoms characterized by glucose intolerance, insufficient insulin release, and elevated proinsulin secretion.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of the study's findings.

claim: MSGs have larger size than ISGs in β cells.
source: This comprehensive analysis enables us to separate ISGs from MSGs clearly and to conclude that MSGs have larger size in β cells (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by FIB-SEM data in Figure 4.

claim: Homotypic fusion exists in endocrine β cells.
source: Together with data from in vitro ISG fusion assay (Figure 5F), these lines of evidence clearly demonstrate the existence of homotypic ISG fusion in endocrine β cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on FIB-SEM and in vitro fusion assay data.

claim: Blockade of ISG homotypic fusion by targeting Syt-IV or STX6 slowed down prohormone processing.
source: Interestingly, blockade of ISG homotypic fusion by targeting Syt-IV or STX6 slowed down prohormone processing (Ahras et al., 2006; Wendler et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to previous studies.

claim: PC1/3 and PC2 are strictly pH-dependent.
source: Specifically, PC1/3 and PC2, which process proinsulin, are strictly pH-dependent (Lamango et al., 1999; Orci et al., 1994; Seidah et al., 1993; Smeekens et al., 1992; Steiner, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to previous studies.

claim: Granule acidification is blocked in the absence of HID-1.
source: Indeed, we have provided the first evidence that granule acidification is blocked in the absence of HID-1 (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by DAMP and Lysosensor data in Figure 6.

claim: HID-1 KO inhibits ISG homotypic fusion and thereby blocks granule acidification, which impairs the pH-dependent activity of PCs and retards proinsulin processing.
source: Hence, it is plausible that HID-1 KO inhibits ISG homotypic fusion and thereby blocks granule acidification, which impairs the pH-dependent activity of PCs and retards proinsulin processing.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation stated in the discussion based on the study's findings.

claim: Progressive granule acidification is driven by the vacuolar H+-ATPase.
source: Progressive granule acidification is driven by the vacuolar H+-ATPase, which transports protons into the lumen and causes a decrease of the intragranular pH (Jefferies et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Vacuolar H+-ATPase was present on ISGs as well as on MSGs.
source: We verified that vacuolar H+-ATPase was present on ISGs as well as on MSGs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by Western blot data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Homotypic ISG fusion plays a pivotal role during SG maturation by condensing not only prohormones but also membrane machinery components, such as vacuolar H+-ATPase.
source: We propose that homotypic ISG fusion plays a pivotal role during SG maturation by condensing not only prohormones but also membrane machinery components, such as vacuolar H+-ATPase, which are required for the acidification of prohormones and their processing to form active peptides.
evidence: This is a proposed model stated in the discussion based on the study's findings.

claim: Blockade of homotypic ISG fusion arrests SGs in an immature state and impairs subsequent maturation steps such as acidification, processing and sorting.
source: Blockade of homotypic ISG fusion arrests SGs in an immature state and impairs subsequent maturation steps such as acidification, processing and sorting.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the study's findings.

claim: Obese type 2 diabetic patients exhibited a greater rise in the proinsulin to insulin ratio than non-diabetic controls after an oral glucose challenge.
source: As early as 1972, Duckworth and Kitabchi reported that obese type 2 diabetic patients exhibited a greater rise in the proinsulin to insulin ratio than non-diabetic controls after an oral glucose challenge (Duckworth and Kitabchi, 1972).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Proinsulin and proinsulin-like compounds in serum have a close relationship with T2DM.
source: In recent years, an increasing amount of experimental and clinical evidence indicates that proinsulin and proinsulin-like compounds (mainly des-31,32 proinsulin) in serum have a close relationship with T2DM, whereas hyperinsulinemia in the early and intermediate disease stages is due to cross-reactivity between insulin and its precursors (Pfutzner et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Genetic variants that affect proinsulin folding and processing result in susceptibility to T2DM.
source: Indeed, genetic variants that affect proinsulin folding and processing result in susceptibility to T2DM (Liu et al., 2010; Zheng et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to previous studies.

claim: HID-1 is a novel player in homotypic ISG fusion.
source: In the current study, we have identified HID-1 as a novel player in homotypic ISG fusion, ablation of which impairs proinsulin processing.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the discussion based on the study's findings.

claim: LRRK2 was found to recruit Rab2 to ISGs for the selective sorting of lysozyme during SG maturation in Paneth cells.
source: In fact LRRK2, a major susceptibility gene for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), was found to recruit Rab2 to ISGs for the selective sorting of lysozyme during SG maturation in Paneth cells (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Hid1 and other genes involved in SG maturation should be considered as candidates for susceptibility for T2DM, IBD and many other diseases involving peptide hormones and neuropeptides.
source: In light of this and other studies (Hatanaka et al., 2011; Katsuta et al., 2015; Stoy et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2015), Hid1 and other genes involved in SG maturation should be considered as previously unappreciated candidates for susceptibility for T2DM, IBD and many other diseases involving peptide hormones and neuropeptides.
evidence: This is a proposal stated in the discussion based on the current study and cited previous studies.

claim: HID-1 is a novel factor that is essential for homotypic fusion of ISGs.
source: In summary, we have identified a novel player that is essential for homotypic fusion of ISGs.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the discussion based on the study's findings.

claim: Homotypic ISG fusion is essential for granule acidification and cargo processing.
source: We provide evidence that homotypic ISG fusion is essential for granule acidification and cargo processing.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the discussion based on the study's findings.

claim: The SGs in peripheral regions were significantly larger than those in the Golgi region in WT β cells.
source: We further compared SG size and found that the SGs in peripheral regions were significantly larger than those in the Golgi region in WT β cells (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by size distribution data in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: The presence of larger SGs in the peripheral regions is consistent with the maturation of SGs on their way from the Golgi to the periphery.
source: The presence of larger SGs in the peripheral regions is consistent with the maturation of SGs on their way from the Golgi to the periphery because it has been reported that ISGs can fuse with each other and become larger in size during maturation (Urbe et al., 1998).
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the results section, supported by the current data and a citation to a previous study.

claim: DAMP accumulates in insulin-containing SGs.
source: We verified that DAMP accumulated in insulin-containing SGs by immunofluorescence co-localization (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6A.

claim: In WT β cells, the grey levels of dense cores are mostly distributed in a zone with higher values (grey level > 190).
source: Our results showed that in WT β cells, the grey levels of dense cores are mostly distributed in a zone with higher values (grey level > 190, designated as denser cores in Figure 4D) and only a small proportion are in a zone with lower values (grey level < 190, designated as lighter cores in Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by FIB-SEM data analysis in Figure 4D.

claim: The lighter core SGs were mostly from the Golgi region (84.0%) in WT β cells.
source: The lighter core SGs were mostly from the Golgi region (84.0%), while the peripheral SGs are almost denser cores (99.2%).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on FIB-SEM data analysis.

claim: The peripheral SGs are almost denser cores (99.2%) in WT β cells.
source: The lighter core SGs were mostly from the Golgi region (84.0%), while the peripheral SGs are almost denser cores (99.2%).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on FIB-SEM data analysis.

claim: There are at least two populations of SGs, ISGs and MSGs in resting WT β cells.
source: This result confirms the existence of at least two populations of SGs, ISGs and MSGs in resting WT β cells, and suggests that only a small fraction of ISGs are in the Golgi region.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the results section based on FIB-SEM data analysis.

claim: Only a small fraction of ISGs are in the Golgi region in WT β cells.
source: This result confirms the existence of at least two populations of SGs, ISGs and MSGs in resting WT β cells, and suggests that only a small fraction of ISGs are in the Golgi region.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the results section based on FIB-SEM data analysis.

claim: In KO cells, the clear distinction between the two populations of SGs was replaced by continuous distribution of grey levels from light to dense values.
source: However, in KO cells, the clear distinction between the two populations was replaced by continuous distribution of grey levels from light to dense values (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by FIB-SEM data analysis in Figure 4E.

claim: Proinsulin-positive ISGs in HID-1 KO cells retain Syt-IV but not VAMP4.
source: Thus, proinsulin-positive ISGs in HID-1 KO cells seem to retain Syt-IV but not VAMP4, suggesting that VAMP4 recruitment to r retention in ISG depends on HID-1.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on co-localization data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: VAMP4 is not an essential component for ISG–ISG fusion process.
source: Besides, a previous study has suggested that VAMP4 is not an essential component for ISG–ISG fusion process (Wendler et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Homotypic fusion events are characterized by the appearance of two dense cores within one limiting membrane.
source: To test this hypothesis, we took advantage of the high three-dimensional (3D) resolution of FIB-SEM to directly visualize homotypic fusion events, which are characterized by the appearance of two dense cores within one limiting membrane (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: GFP-labeled insulins were correctly sorted to SGs as they co-localized with chromogranin A.
source: We verified that these GFP-labeled insulins were correctly sorted to SGs as they co-localized with chromogranin A (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), a marker of insulin-containing SGs.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by co-localization data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Chromogranin A is a marker of insulin-containing SGs.
source: We verified that these GFP-labeled insulins were correctly sorted to SGs as they co-localized with chromogranin A (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), a marker of insulin-containing SGs.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as established knowledge.

claim: The Golgi apparatus in β cells appears like a basket.
source: It has been reported that in some acinar cells, the Golgi apparatus appears like a basket (Koga et al., 2016; Watanabe et al., 2012). Our large volume 3D SEM data of Golgi stacks in β cells showed the same basket shape (Video 3).
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section and supported by 3D SEM data in Video 3, with citations to previous studies.

claim: The basket region encircled by Golgi stacks was defined as the Golgi region.
source: The basket region encircled by Golgi stacks was defined as the Golgi region.
evidence: This is a methodological definition stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: SGs localized within 1 μm of the plasma membrane PM were defined as peripheral.
source: SGs localized within 1 μm of the plasma membrane PM were defined as peripheral.
evidence: This is a methodological definition stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: Rodent insulins are produced from two independent genes called Ins1 and Ins2.
source: Rodent insulins are produced from two independent genes called Ins1 and Ins2.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as established knowledge.

claim: Products from the Ins1 gene are predominant in rats.
source: Insulin1 was analyzed because products from the Ins1 gene are predominant in rats (Gishizky and Grodsky, 1987; Michael et al., 1987) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citations to previous studies.

claim: PC1/3 first acts at the B–C junction to produce the intermediate des-31,32 proinsulin.
source: It has been suggested that PC1/3 first acts at the B–C junction to produce the intermediate des-31,32 proinsulin, whereas PC2 preferentially cleaves at the A–C junction to produce the intermediate des-64,65 proinsulin (Halban and Irminger, 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation to a previous study.

claim: PC2 preferentially cleaves at the A–C junction to produce the intermediate des-64,65 proinsulin.
source: It has been suggested that PC1/3 first acts at the B–C junction to produce the intermediate des-31,32 proinsulin, whereas PC2 preferentially cleaves at the A–C junction to produce the intermediate des-64,65 proinsulin (Halban and Irminger, 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation to a previous study.

claim: The retarded appearance of both des-31,32 and des-64,65 Proinsulin1 during the chase period indicated the concurrent impairment of PC1/3 and PC2 function in the KO INS-1 cells.
source: The retarded appearance of both des-31,32 and des-64,65 Proinsulin1 during the chase period indicated the concurrent impairment of PC1/3 and PC2 function in the KO INS-1 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the results section based on LC-MS data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: CPE is an enzyme that catalyzes the release of C-terminal arginine or lysine residues from polypeptides.
source: CPE is an enzyme that catalyzes the release of C-terminal arginine or lysine residues from polypeptides.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as established knowledge.

claim: ISGs exhibit lighter dense cores than MSGs.
source: It has been suggested that ISGs exhibit lighter dense cores than MSGs (Furuta et al., 1998; Wijesekara et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citations to previous studies.

claim: Acidification is one of the most important steps in proinsulin processing and granule maturation.
source: It has been demonstrated that acidification is one of the most important steps in proinsulin processing and granule maturation (Orci et al., 1986).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to a previous study.

claim: ISG homotypic fusion could increase the density of the vacuolar H+-ATPase, as well as decreasing the H+ permeability.
source: Although it is not clear how homotypic ISG fusion causes granule acidification, it has been proposed that ISG–ISG fusion could increase the density of the vacuolar H+-ATPase, as well as decreasing the H+ permeability (Wu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Maturation of SGs may not always come with an increase in diameter.
source: Please note that maturation of SGs may not always come with an increase in diameter, MSGs can either become smaller or larger than ISGs (Tooze et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Maturation involves membrane remodeling steps of both homotypic fusion and budding events.
source: Maturation involves membrane remodeling steps of both homotypic fusion and budding events.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as established knowledge.

claim: Homotypic fusion would result in an increase in the size of ISGs.
source: Homotypic fusion would result in an increase in the size of ISGs, whereas budding of clathrin-coated vesicles from ISG would allow removal of excessive membrane and reduction in size (Arvan and Castle, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Budding of clathrin-coated vesicles from ISG would allow removal of excessive membrane and reduction in size.
source: Homotypic fusion would result in an increase in the size of ISGs, whereas budding of clathrin-coated vesicles from ISG would allow removal of excessive membrane and reduction in size (Arvan and Castle, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to a previous study.

claim: The size of MSGs is determined by the coordinated action of fusion and budding events and is likely to be a cell-specific property.
source: Hence, the size of MSGs is determined by the coordinated action of fusion and budding events and is likely to be a cell-specific property.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the discussion based on the understanding of SG maturation processes.

claim: The interaction between Munc18-1 and syntaxin 1 is critical for the docking and priming of synaptic vesicles.
source: The interaction between Munc18-1, a neuronal SM protein, and syntaxin 1 is critical for the docking and priming of synaptic vesicles, which also requires Munc13 proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as established knowledge.

claim: The MUN domain dramatically accelerates the transition from the closed syntaxin 1–Munc18-1 complex to the SNARE complex.
source: It has been proposed that the MUN domain dramatically accelerates the transition from the closed syntaxin 1–Munc18-1 complex to the SNARE complex, probably by extracting the SNARE motif of syntaxin 1 from the closed conformation and providing a template for SNARE complex assembly (Ma et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to previous studies.

claim: The MUN domain has a similar architecture to domains found in vesicle tethering factors such as Sec6, Tip20, and Exo70.
source: Structural analyses have shown that the MUN domain has a similar architecture to domains found in vesicle tethering factors such as Sec6, Tip20, and Exo70 (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Munc13s and CAPS belong to a family named CATHCR (complex associated with tethering containing helical rods).
source: As such, Munc13s and CAPS belong to a family named CATHCR (complex associated with tethering containing helical rods) (Rizo and Sudhof, 2012; Yu and Hughson, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to previous studies.

claim: CATCHR proteins have general function(s) in vesicle fusion by providing a physical link between donor and target membranes.
source: CATCHR proteins have general function(s) in vesicle fusion by providing a physical link between donor and target membranes (sometimes called docking and sometimes called tethering) (Yu and Hughson, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Tethering factors bind to SNARE proteins and can accelerate SNARE complex assembly.
source: Moreover, as described above for Munc13-1 and for the HOPS complex, tethering factors bind to SNARE proteins and can accelerate SNARE complex assembly (Ren et al., 2009; Wickner, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to previous studies.

claim: The docking and assembly of the SNARE complex may be mediated by similar but not identical mechanisms in different systems.
source: These ﬁndings suggest that the docking and assembly of the SNARE complex may be mediated by similar but not identical mechanisms in different systems.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the discussion based on cited previous studies.

claim: HID-1 localizes to ISGs.
source: As HID-1 localizes to ISGs, it will be intriguing to test whether HID-1 can serve as a tethering factor to bridge disparate ISG membrane or as a priming factor for SNARE complex assembly.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an established finding from the study.

claim: It will be intriguing to test whether HID-1 can serve as a tethering factor to bridge disparate ISG membrane or as a priming factor for SNARE complex assembly.
source: As HID-1 localizes to ISGs, it will be intriguing to test whether HID-1 can serve as a tethering factor to bridge disparate ISG membrane or as a priming factor for SNARE complex assembly.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the discussion about future research directions.

claim: The large volume SEM and in vitro fusion assays provide the first evidence of ISG homotypic fusion during the maturation of insulin granules.
source: The large volume SEM and in vitro fusion assays we developed here provide the first evidence of ISG homotypic fusion during the maturation of insulin granules.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the discussion highlighting the novelty of the study's findings.

claim: Processing of proinsulin to insulin and C-peptide by the endoproteases PC1/3 and PC2 during ISG maturation allows insulin to condense.
source: However, processing of proinsulin to insulin and C-peptide by the endoproteases PC1/3 and PC2 during ISG maturation allows insulin to condense (Arvan et al., 1991).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Proinsulin does not efficiently pack into the higher-order granule matrix.
source: Nascent ISGs generated from the TGN contain proinsulin, which does not efficiently pack into the higher-order granule matrix (Steiner, 1973).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to a previous study.

claim: HID-1 KO impairs proinsulin processing.
source: In the current study, we show for the first time that HID-1 KO impairs proinsulin processing (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: HID-1 deficiency does not block DCV exocytosis but causes defective insulin signaling in both mouse and worm.
source: This answers the long-standing question of why HID-1 deficiency does not block DCV exocytosis (Mesa et al., 2011) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) but causes defective insulin signaling in both mouse and worm (Ailion and Thomas, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion, integrating the current study's findings with cited previous studies.
